clinicalPearls: CLL is a monoclonal proliferation of mature B lymphocytes defined by an absolute clonal B-cell count of ≥5 × 10⁹/L in the blood; it is a disease of older adults (median age at diagnosis 71) (p.849).

Most commonly diagnosed incidentally on routine blood work showing an elevated lymphocyte count in an asymptomatic individual; the natural history is heterogeneous, with some patients never requiring therapy (p.849, p.853).

On the peripheral blood smear, the small lymphocytes are increased and many rupture during smear preparation, leaving nuclear material without surrounding cytoplasm — smudge cells, which are rare in the absence of chronic lymphoid leukemia (p.443).

Diagnosis is confirmed by flow cytometry on peripheral blood; the typical immunophenotype is CD19+, CD20+, CD22+, CD23+, CD200+, the T-cell marker CD5+, and dim surface immunoglobulin (kappa or lambda). A clonal B-cell count ≥5 × 10⁹/L needs no further workup to confirm CLL (p.852).

Small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) is the tissue-based counterpart of CLL (lymphadenopathy/splenomegaly with a small clonal blood population); genetic and molecular features are identical and SLL is managed identically to CLL (p.852).

Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL) is a precursor: clonal B cells below the CLL threshold without nodal/organ involvement or cytopenias; high-count MBL progresses to overt CLL at ~1–2% per year, whereas low-count MBL has a negligible progression rate (p.849, p.852).

IGHV mutational status is a key prognostic factor: ~60% have IGHV ≥2% mutated from germline (more indolent course), while ~40% are IGHV-unmutated (more rapid progression, shorter survival before BCR-targeted therapy) (p.850).
B-cell receptor (BCR) signaling is central to CLL pathogenesis, characterized by low-level IgM expression and tonic activation of antiapoptotic pathways promoting tumor survival (p.850).
FISH (with or without karyotype) should be checked before every line of therapy because cytogenetics can evolve even without treatment, mainly to detect acquisition of del(17)(p13.1) (p.851).
Bone marrow biopsy is not undertaken until therapy is initiated, except in cases of unexplained cytopenias; CT imaging is usually unnecessary at diagnosis (p.854).
A watchful-waiting strategy is used for most patients, with therapy reserved for symptomatic disease, as multiple trials show no survival advantage to earlier therapy (p.854).

Hypogammaglobulinemia affects all immunoglobulin subclasses and occurs in ~85% of patients at some point; low IgG and IgA correlate with infection risk, but isolated IgM reduction does not seem to confer excess infection risk (p.852).
harrison.pathophysiology: CLL is a monoclonal expansion of mature B lymphocytes; the definitive cell of origin is not established (mature/memory B cell, stepwise transformation, or hematopoietic stem cell are all proposed). Distinct BCR signaling — low-level IgM, tonic antiapoptotic pathway activation — drives tumor survival, with upregulation of BCR-pathway genes in lymph nodes and marrow versus blood. The CLL genome is relatively simple (~20 nonsynonymous and ~5 structural changes) with no unifying driver; recurrent mutations include SF3B1, NOTCH1, MYD88, ATM, and TP53 (mostly enriched in IGHV-unmutated disease, except MYD88 which favors IGHV-mutated/indolent disease). Key cytogenetic lesions: del(13)(q14.3) (sole, indolent; causes loss of the miR15/16 cluster that normally suppresses BCL2 and other antiapoptotic genes), trisomy 12 (intermediate), del(11)(q22.3)/ATM (bulky disease, aggressive), and del(17)(p13.1)/TP53 (poorest prognosis). Immune dysregulation pervades the disease: innate defects (reduced complement, neutrophil and NK cell defects), adaptive defects (CD4+ T-cell exhaustion, Th1-to-Th2 shift, expanded T regulatory cells), nurse-like tumor-associated macrophages, and humoral hypogammaglobulinemia (p.849-852).
additionalDifferentials: Mantle cell lymphoma (CD5+, but CD23-negative, cyclin D1+, moderate/bright CD20 and surface Ig) — distinguished by immunophenotype (p.852)
Marginal zone lymphoma (CD5 -/+, CD23 -/+, bright surface Ig) (p.852)
Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (clonal B cells below the CLL threshold without organ involvement or cytopenias) (p.852)
Small lymphocytic lymphoma (tissue-based counterpart with identical molecular features) (p.852)
B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia arising from CLL (clinically and therapeutically distinct, though classified under Richter's transformation) (p.853-854)
infectionMimics: Reactive lymphocytosis from viral infection — viral infections produce larger reactive lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm, in contrast to the increased small lymphocytes and smudge cells of CLL (p.443)
nonInfectiousMimics: Other CD5+ or low-grade B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders (mantle cell, marginal zone, follicular lymphoma) distinguishable by flow cytometry immunophenotype, morphology, or cytogenetics (p.852)
additionalInvestigations: Flow cytometry of peripheral blood for the characteristic immunophenotype (CD19, CD20, CD22, CD23, CD200, CD5, dim surface Ig) — diagnostic test of choice (p.852)
FISH for recurrent abnormalities del(13)(q14.3), trisomy 12, del(11)(q22.3), del(17)(p13.1); repeated before each line of therapy to detect acquired del(17p) (p.851)
Stimulated metaphase karyotype, including assessment for complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities) (p.851)
Sequencing for TP53 and IGHV mutational status for prognostication (p.854)
β2-microglobulin and LDH (prognostic; component of CLL International Prognostic Index) (p.853-854)
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test for warm IgG antibody when autoimmune hemolytic anemia is suspected (Coombs-negative cases can occur) (p.853)
Reticulocyte count, bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin to evaluate suspected hemolysis (p.853)

18FDG-PET/CT to localize a biopsy site when Richter's transformation is suspected (SUV <5 consistent with CLL; SUV >5 suspicious; ≥10 very concerning); excisional biopsy preferred over fine-needle aspiration (p.853-854)
CLL International Prognostic Index integrating TP53 status, IGHV status, β2-microglobulin, clinical stage, and age (p.854)
redFlags: Richter's transformation — transformation to an aggressive lymphoma (most commonly DLBCL; Hodgkin lymphoma is a recognized variant). Suspect with rapid progression of adenopathy (often localized), constitutional symptoms (fatigue, night sweats, fever, weight loss), and usually high LDH (p.853-854)
del(17)(p13.1)/TP53 loss or mutation — poorest prognosis, rapid progression, poor response to DNA-damaging therapy (p.850-851)
Complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities) — adverse impact on time to treatment and overall survival, worsening with increasing complexity (p.851)
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia — death from uncontrolled AIHA can occur without appropriate supportive care; immediate therapy is almost always necessary (p.853)

Symptoms indicating need for therapy: progressive marrow failure, massive/progressive/symptomatic splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, lymphocyte doubling time <6 months, autoimmune cytopenia unresponsive to standard therapy, or constitutional symptoms (p.854)
harrison.prognosis: Heterogeneous: many patients are asymptomatic and never require therapy while others need multiple lines and die of disease. Overall survival has improved markedly (5-year OS 70% in 1980, 92% in 2015, likely higher today), and only a small minority now die of CLL itself. Infections cause ~30–50% of CLL-related deaths. Favorable markers: IGHV-mutated disease, sole del(13)(q14.3), MYD88 mutation. Adverse markers: IGHV-unmutated disease, del(17p)/TP53, del(11q)/ATM, NOTCH1, complex karyotype, and high β2-microglobulin/LDH. The CLL International Prognostic Index stratifies 5-year survival from ~93% (low risk) to ~23% (very high risk) in training-set data, though it has not been validated in the era of novel targeted therapies. Richter's transformation carries a poor prognosis, with median survival of 6–16 months for clonally related DLBCL versus ~5 years for clonally unrelated lymphomas (p.849, p.851, p.853-854).
pitfalls: When anemia or thrombocytopenia appear, distinguish autoimmune cytopenia from marrow replacement — the therapeutic approaches differ, and autoimmune cytopenias often respond without treating the underlying CLL (p.853)
AIHA can be Coombs-negative, so a negative direct antiglobulin test does not exclude it (p.853)

ITP can be hard to distinguish from disease progression because no lab test directly identifies the platelet-destruction mechanism; isolated thrombocytopenia and rapid platelet decline without alternative cause point to ITP (p.853)

del(13)(q14.3) seen on banded karyotype (rather than only on FISH) indicates a larger deletion involving the retinoblastoma gene, which negates the favorable prognosis usually associated with this marker (p.850)
Live vaccines should be avoided in CLL because of the small risk of viral reactivation in an immunocompromised host (p.853)
Fine-needle aspiration should be discouraged for diagnosing suspected Richter's transformation; excisional biopsy is preferred (p.854)
Cytogenetics can change without therapy, so prior FISH results may be outdated — recheck before each line of treatment (p.851)
harrison.severityClassification: Two staging systems, both based on physical exam and labs (no imaging or marrow required). Rai system (more common in the US): low risk (stage 0) = lymphocytosis only; intermediate risk (stage I/II) = lymphocytosis with lymphadenopathy, with or without splenomegaly/hepatomegaly; high risk (stage III/IV) = lymphocytosis with anemia or thrombocytopenia from marrow involvement. Binet system (more common in Europe): A = <3 areas of lymphadenopathy; B = ≥3 areas of lymphadenopathy; C = hemoglobin ≤10 g/dL and/or platelets <100,000/μL. The CLL International Prognostic Index refines outcome prediction using TP53 status, IGHV status, β2-microglobulin, clinical stage, and age (p.854).
